system_overview: This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, which appeared in 'Solution of a Problem in Concurrent Programming Control' in Communications of the ACM, September 1965. This was the first algorithm to solve the mutual exclusion problem for N concurrent processes using only shared variables, founding the study of concurrent algorithms. The algorithm uses two boolean arrays and a shared integer to coordinate access to a critical section.
actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of concurrent processes. Each process repeatedly cycles through four phases: non-critical section, entry protocol, critical section, and exit protocol. All processes compete for mutually exclusive access to a single shared critical section.
state_variables: The system maintains: (1) a boolean array with one entry per process, initially all true, which a process sets to false when it begins the entry protocol and resets to true when it exits the critical section; (2) a second boolean array with one entry per process, initially all true, used during the entry protocol to signal readiness -- a process sets it to true when yielding priority and to false when asserting priority; (3) a single shared integer identifying one distinguished process, initially set to an arbitrary process. Each process also has a local temporary variable used to iterate over other processes during the entry protocol.
initial_state: Both boolean arrays have all entries set to true. The shared integer is set to an arbitrary process from the process set. All processes begin at the start of their non-critical section. Each process's local temporary variable is uninitialized.
actions: Each process cycles through these steps: (1) The process sets its first boolean flag to false, signaling it wants to enter the critical section. (2) The process checks whether it is the currently distinguished process (the shared integer). If not, it yields by setting its second boolean flag to true, then reads the distinguished process's first boolean flag: if that flag is true (the distinguished process is idle), the process claims the distinguished role by writing its own identity to the shared integer. It then loops back to recheck. (3) If the process is the distinguished process, it sets its second boolean flag to false, asserting priority. It then iterates over all other processes, checking each one's second boolean flag. If any other process also has its second flag set to false (also asserting priority), the process goes back to step 2. (4) If no other process is asserting priority, the process enters the critical section. (5) Upon exiting, the process resets its second boolean flag to true and its first boolean flag to true, then returns to the non-critical section.
safety_properties: Mutual exclusion: at most one process is in the critical section at any time.
liveness_properties: Deadlock freedom: if some process is trying to enter the critical section, then eventually some process (not necessarily the same one) enters the critical section. The algorithm is NOT starvation-free: it is possible for a process to wait indefinitely while other processes repeatedly enter the critical section.
model_bounds: The set of processes is declared as a constant. For model checking, it must be instantiated with a specific finite set (a 3-process model has about 90,000 reachable states; a 4-process model has about 33 million).
additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each process's next-state action, ensuring that no process halts permanently if it can always take a step. A stronger specification variant restricts fairness to apply only when the process is not in its non-critical section, allowing processes to remain in their non-critical sections indefinitely (modeling voluntary idleness). Under this stronger variant, a correspondingly stronger deadlock-freedom property is required that accounts for processes anywhere in the entry protocol, not just at the initial step.
